issues.title: Egypt: Investigating severe broadband throttling after monthly data caps
issues.body:
**

# Egypt: Investigating severe broadband throttling after monthly data caps

Hello everyone,

I'm looking for technical insights into residential broadband throttling in Egypt.

**ISP:** Telecom Egypt (WE)

**Issue:** After the monthly data allowance is exhausted, some residential plans are reduced to approximately **256 Kbps**.

WE also advertises special access arrangements for certain educational and government websites. Examples include:

- https://digital.gov.eg
- https://mcit.gov.eg
- https://tra.gov.eg
- https://www.ekb.eg
- https://maharatech.gov.eg

The exact behavior of these exemptions after quota exhaustion may vary.

I would appreciate technical guidance on the following questions:

1. How can users distinguish an account-wide bandwidth limit from traffic-specific throttling?
2. What privacy-preserving tests could determine whether certain services retain higher speeds?
3. Are there legitimate VPN or network optimizations that improve usability on a 256 Kbps connection?
4. Are there existing open-source tools or research projects that investigate comparable ISP policies?

I understand that a VPN cannot necessarily remove a hard account-level speed cap.

My goal is to understand the technical restrictions and identify practical, measurable improvements.

For personal safety reasons, I prefer to remain anonymous and ask that no personally identifying information be requested publicly.

Thank you for any technical insights or references.

**

issues.title: Nakis: a TLS tunnel proxy built around connection reuse and write coalescing (efficiency first, circumvention effect unverified)
issues.body:
Hello all,

I would like to share a small project and ask for feedback from people who know this area better than I do. Nakis is a SOCKS5-in, TLS-tunnel-out proxy written in Go. Its main goal is transfer efficiency: get a ready tunnel to the application with as little waiting as possible, and keep per-write overhead low. Resistance to DPI was a secondary concern. I have not tested it against any real censor, so please read the DPI-related parts as hypotheses.

Repo: https://github.com/n-yarvex/nakis (MIT). The wire format and notes on the reference implementation are in doc/SPEC.md.

## Where the waiting goes

Most browser sessions are short, so the cost is dominated by setting up a tunnel: TCP, TLS, then whatever authentication the protocol adds. Nakis tries to take that off the critical path.

**Pre-connected pool.** The client keeps tunnels that have already finished the TLS handshake and authentication. A new session takes one from the pool and starts sending right away. This is always on, because turning it off could only make things slower.

**Reuse.** When a session ends, each side sends a zero-length frame (called NAP in the spec) for its own direction. Once both have been seen, no error occurred, and the tunnel has not used up its lifespan, it goes back to the pool and the next session reuses it without a new handshake. Each tunnel draws its own lifespan: a number of sessions (by default between 4 and 8) and a byte budget (log-uniform between 8 and 256 MiB), so there is no fixed "Nth session" or "Nth byte" boundary.

**Racing when the pool is empty.** The client dials several candidate addresses: the first two immediately, the rest staggered by 50 ms. The first to finish the handshake serves the session. The others are not thrown away; they go into the pool. The idea is mostly for lossy links and servers with several addresses, where one slow path should not stall everything.

## Write coalescing

Many proxies write each application read as its own frame. Nakis puts a queue (a "Box") in front of the tunnel and decides when to flush ("Gate"). One frame is one Write, which under TLS ends up in one record.

- If the queue is empty and the last data arrived at least 40 µs ago, the chunk is sent immediately. This is meant to keep interactive small writes from being delayed.
- Otherwise chunks queue up and are packed greedily into one frame, up to `send_pack`. A chunk is never split; what does not fit waits for the next frame.
- The queue is flushed when it reaches `send_pack`, or comes within `send_tail` bytes (default 512) of it.
- If it is not full, a 250 µs timer runs. If more data arrived in the meantime, it waits another tick, up to `send_quiet` x 4 ticks. With `send_quiet=4` that means at most about 4 ms of merging while data keeps arriving, and at most 250 µs once it stops.
- Large reads (32766 bytes or more) bypass the queue after flushing what is already queued, to keep ordering.
- The server has a second layer: small upstream frames are merged into writes of up to `merge_pack` (default 20 KiB) towards the target. When the queue reaches `max_queue`, the server stops reading the tunnel and TCP backpressure slows the client.

The trade-off is plain: under sustained small writes, latency can rise by up to `send_quiet` milliseconds in exchange for fewer, larger records.

## Shaping the first packets

The first few packets of a session (up to eight per direction) get a randomly drawn target size, per tunnel, per session, per direction. The target is reached by coalescing application data first. Padding (a frame with length 0xFFFF) is only used if the data has not filled the target after 2 ms, so this does not work like a conventional padding scheme. For the first packet only, that wait is an added latency of up to 2 ms. The plan also looks at the destination port: for ports that usually carry TLS (443 and similar), it covers more packets and draws larger ones more often, on the guess that a TLS handshake is nested insi

* ["Throttling Twitter: an emerging censorship technique in Russia"](https://censorbib.nymity.ch/#Xue2021a) (2021)
* OONI [Throttling measurement methodology](https://github.com/ooni/probe-cli/blob/b5a5b6f0e7868c6e617711a0cb9521afb41c7849/docs/design/dd-007-throttling.md)

Do you know anything about the nature of how the throttling is implemented? For example, if you run an ICMP echo (ping) test at a high rate while being throttled, does it show higher packet loss, higher round-trip times, or both?

If the throttling relies on, for example, TCP congestion behavior under packet loss, then there may be possibilities such as using non-TCP protocols.

comments.issue_title: [Russia] recent mass ip bans
comments.body:
Adding a few data points from Tatarstan, Russia (home ISPs: Rostelecom / Tattelecom / Dom.ru), measured September–November 2026.

**Hetzner is fully unreachable, not throttled.** From an ER-Telecom line, TCP connect to Hetzner succeeds (both Helsinki 95.217.255.81 and the German corporate range 213.133.116.44), but the TLS handshake is killed — `openssl s_client` returns no certificate, and HTTPS downloads return 0 bytes at any request size, including 8 KB. Vultr, Linode and Cloudflare were reachable from the same line at the same time. Scaleway behaved like Hetzner.

**Geo databases can disagree with hoster jurisdiction.** netcup (AS214996) resolves as **US** in both ipinfo and iplocation, despite being a German company. Worth checking if the exit country matters for your use case — it is not visible from the hoster's own description.

**Two measurement pitfalls that produced wrong conclusions on my side:**

- Cloudflare's speedtest endpoint returns **HTTP 403** from proxy addresses. The 1-byte response looks exactly like a censorship freeze at ~16 MB. I initially misread this as TSPU throttling of the node. Leaseweb and RWTH mirrors behave correctly and showed full 16 MB transfers through the same tunnel at the same moment.
- `nc -z` on macOS reports "closed" for known-good hosts (1.1.1.1, Yandex), so it is unusable for reachability testing here. `curl --resolve` and `openssl s_client` give correct results.

**SNI/IP correlation.** A commercial service I observed keeps its Reality SNI donor domain **in the same /24** as its Russian entry node, while its foreign node has no such correlation. Possibly a deliberate response to SNI/IP mismatch checks.

Questions, if anyone has data:

1. What is the typical lifetime of a foreign VPS address under personal load (1–3 devices, no resale) — weeks or months? Is there a hoster-dependent difference in address lifetime specifically, as opposed to latency?
2. Does keeping the Reality SNI donor in the same subnet/ASN as the server measurably help right now?
3. For a Russia-based entry relay, which providers survive longest in practice?

Happy to run specific tests from this vantage point if that would be useful.

issues.title: Fix end address of 198.18.0.0/15 in IsInReservedRange
issues.body:
The RFC 2544 benchmarking range in `IsInReservedRange` ends at `192.19.255.255` instead of `198.19.255.255`. Since the end is below the start, the `first <= ip <= last` check never matches, so 198.18.0.0/15 is not treated as reserved even with `reservedrange = true`.

Checked by calling `i2p::util::net::IsInReservedRange` from a `libi2pd.a` built at tag 3.0.0:

```
                 before         after
198.18.0.1       not reserved   reserved
198.19.255.254   not reserved   reserved
192.19.0.1       not reserved   not reserved
10.1.2.3         reserved       reserved
8.8.8.8          not reserved   not reserved
```

The typo is also in 2.59.0.

comments.issue_title: Memory leak in torrents tunnel (3.0.0): ~600 MB/h anon growth while torrents are active, not released on stop
comments.body:
## Update: root cause found, fix + PR

Thanks for the hint about DHT, LeaseSets and tags — agreed, memory staying flat after `torrent-stop` alone doesn't prove a leak. The growth happens while torrents are **active**, and I traced it in the source. PR: https://github.com/PurpleI2P/i2pd/pull/2635

### Root cause

1. `Piece::BlockReceived()` allocates a buffer of the **full piece size** when the first block of a piece arrives.
2. When the download of that piece is interrupted (peer chokes, connection terminates, requests time out → `HandleChokeMsg()`, `PeerConnection::Terminate()`, `Piece::Reset()` after `PIECE_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT`), an **incomplete** piece only gets its requests cleared. `m_Data` is kept; `Reset()` frees the buffer only for *complete* pieces.
3. `Torrent::GetNextBlockToRequest()` picks rarest-first among non-requested pieces and does **not prefer already started pieces**. Other connections start new pieces while abandoned partial pieces keep their buffers indefinitely. With frequent chokes/disconnects on I2P this grows linearly.
4. `TorrentsTunnel::HandleTorrentsStatusUpdateTimer()` skips stopped torrents, so their buffers are never released.

This is still the case on current `openssl`.

While porting the fix to `openssl` I found a related regression: since the switch to `Blocks`/`dynamic_bitset`, `Piece::InvalidateAllBlocks()` only resets existing blocks. A piece that was already marked complete (`m_Blocks == nullptr`) — after a **hash mismatch** or a **failed save** — stays "complete" without data and is never downloaded again, while bitfield and resume file report it as available.

### Fix (PR <PR-LINK>, against `openssl`)

- **Prefer started pieces** in `GetNextBlockToRequest()`, so partial pieces get completed instead of abandoned.
- **Release abandoned partial pieces:** new `Piece::ReleasePartialData()` drops buffer and received blocks of an incomplete piece without outstanding requests after `PIECE_PARTIAL_DATA_TIMEOUT` (300 s) of inactivity, immediately if the torrent is stopped.
- **Clean up stopped and idle complete torrents:** the status timer calls the new `Torrent::ReleaseInactivePieces()` for them.
- **`m_IsSaving`** keeps a completed piece's buffer alive from verification until the disk IO thread has written all fragments (`Dump()` toggled `m_IsSending` per fragment, so the buffer could be freed between fragments).
- **`InvalidateAllBlocks()`** recreates the blocks of a piece marked complete, so it is downloaded again; the failed-save path posts this back to the tunnel thread.

Trade-off: blocks of a partial piece are discarded after 300 s without activity (or on stop) and requested again later — at most a few pieces per torrent.

The PR builds cleanly against current `openssl` (make, g++ / Boost 1.83, Debian 13).

### Results

Same host, 6 torrents, `anon` memory of the i2pd cgroup, sampled every 5 minutes. The fixed run used 3.0.0 with this fix plus a few small follow-up changes (DHT table limits, `GetInfo()` without copy, faster piece selection) which I'll propose separately; they don't touch piece buffer handling.

| | 3.0.0 | 3.0.0 + fix |
|---|---|---|
| growth after warm-up | **~600 MB/h**, linear (234 → 1496 MB in 90 min) | **~150 MB/h** (452 → 528 MB, 13:26–13:56) |
| traffic per direction | much lower (not logged) | 3–4 MB/s |
| peers | 61–71 | 46–56 |
| restarts / OOM | — | none |

LeaseSets and incoming ECIES tags of the torrents destination were logged as well. They go up and down rather than growing: `ls` 177–410, `ecIn` 150k–350k. Between 13:31 and 13:56 `ecIn` stayed almost flat (290k → 299k) while `anon` grew by 72 MB, so tags are not the growth source.

The remaining ~150 MB/h coincide with more open connections (`fd` 560 → 996) and transit tunnels (362 → 962), so part of it is load. I'm still watching whether it levels off. If it doesn't, glibc heap fragmentation from the frequent 1–16 MB piece buffer allocations would be my next suspect (`MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_=131072` to test

issues.title: VLESS: run multiplexing directly on transport
issues.body:
Move multiplexing to `proxy/vless/multiplex` and Reverse to `proxy/vless/reverse`. VLESS inbound, outbound and Reverse use direct transport paths. Intermediate pipes are removed from all VLESS Multiplex and Reverse paths and from the VMess Multiplex inbound adapter.

Configure VLESS outbound through `settings.multiplex`. The old generic outbound Mux and classic Reverse paths are removed.

Preserve incremental TCP delivery, whole UDP packets and XUDP reconnection. Simplify shutdown and VMess response startup, and retain actual framing and transport errors.

First working version for review.

issues.title: XHTTP: bound TLS handshakes on TCP connections
issues.body:
The ChatGPT desktop app stopped loading workspace settings after an upgrade from one Wayrill version to the next. Restarting Wayrill routing, which restarted Xray, restored access. The traffic log showed the expected policy group, which includes XHTTP over TLS/HTTP/2 outbounds. The app reconnected normally as soon as the next upgrade, to Wayrill 0.37.17 with this patch, finished. The original capture begins after startup, so the evidence for the TLS stall comes from the controlled reproduction below.

## Reproduction and relation to #6590

The loopback reproduction uses an Xray VLESS/XHTTP client and server with the default three XMUX clients. A TCP relay accepts the first three connections, reads each TLS ClientHello and leaves those sockets open without sending a ServerHello. The relay forwards every new connection to the healthy Xray server. HTTP/2 requests sharing a pending dial keep waiting on the old sockets, even after the original application requests time out. Fresh requests then fail despite a working server being available to fresh dials.

This is the same stalled handshake reported in #6590. The additional finding is that the failure can persist across application retries after the peer is healthy for new connections. A TCP stack can keep acknowledging probes while the application or an intermediary makes no progress on a particular TLS handshake. The reproduction uses default TCP keepalive settings and injects a transient fault in the relay. [Closing discussion](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/6590#issuecomment-5178980812)

## Fix

Start a ten-second child context once the TCP connection is established, using the same handshake budget as Go's default HTTP transport. Complete standard TLS explicitly and use the same context for uTLS and REALITY. On expiry the stalled handshake ends and releases the socket, so HTTP/2 can retire the shared pending dial and subsequent requests can dial again. The context ends at handshake completion. Established streams continue under the existing HTTP request lifetime, and HTTP/3 uses QUIC's own handshake timeout.

## Validation

- On upstream `main` at `5d17b872`, six fresh requests timed out over 10.5 seconds. The relay saw no new dials. Restarting the client core restored traffic.
- With the patch, all three stalled sockets closed and a fresh request returned HTTP 200 in the same process. Verified this with Go TLS, uTLS and REALITY over HTTP/2. Also verified that the stalled sockets closed over HTTP/1.1.
- Verified healthy streams transferred data after 12 seconds in each of those configurations. The XHTTP Go suite passed alongside a local regression covering all three TLS paths against silent peers.

issues.title: [Feature] XMC: Yggdrasil third-party login + texture signature verification / XMC 支持 Yggdrasil 第三方登录与材质签名验证
issues.body:
> Status: proposal / ready for discussion. Branch: `feat/xmc-yggdrasil-login` (based on `c4561418`), commits `109e8d2c` + `74eb4feb`.
> 状态：提案，欢迎讨论。分支：`feat/xmc-yggdrasil-login`（基于 `c4561418`），提交 `109e8d2c` + `74eb4feb`。

---

## 中文

### 背景与动机

当前 XMC 的登录认证是自造的：

- 客户端配置里手工填写 `username` / `uuid` / `texturesValue` / `texturesSignature`（需要自己去 Mojang 或皮肤站查 UUID、拉签名材质再复制进配置）；
- 服务端用预共享 `password`（同时作为 RSA 私钥的派生种子）加静态 `profiles` 白名单校验；
- Verify Token 尾部追加预共享密码，和 Minecraft 协议本身没有关系。

维护成本高，且无法复用 Minecraft 生态已有的标准在线模式认证（Yggdrasil / authlib-injector / Blessing Skin）。更重要的是，**如果后续要给 MC 模组实现 XMC 服务端**（让真实 MC 客户端或服务端模组走标准 Yggdrasil 登录接入 XMC），预共享密码模型无法对接，因为模组侧只会实现标准的 `authenticate` / `join` / `hasJoined` 流程。

本次改动把 XMC 改成标准 Yggdrasil 登录客户端 + 标准 `hasJoined` 服务端校验，并补上材质签名验证，为后续 MC 模组实现 XMC 服务端铺路，也为 XMC 客户端将来接入真实 MC 服务端打基础。

### 修改内容

涉及文件：

- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/yggdrasil.go`（新增：Yggdrasil HTTP 客户端、登录/刷新/join/hasJoined、验签）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/client.go`（Yggdrasil 登录、标准 hash、材质验签接入）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/server.go`（hasJoined 校验、随机密钥、断连语义）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/profile.go`（多 properties 读写、身份/材质比较）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/config.go`、`config.proto`、`config.pb.go`
- `infra/conf/transport_finalmask.go`（`yggdrasil` 配置解析、随机密钥生成、警告输出）
- 测试：`yggdrasil_test.go`、`profile_test.go`、`handshake_test.go`、`infra/conf/transport_finalmask_xmc_test.go`

#### 1. 配置

XMC `settings` 新增可选的 `yggdrasil` 段：

```json
{
  "type": "xmc",
  "settings": {
    "hostname": "mc.example.com",
    "yggdrasil": {
      "api": "https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil",
      "username": "user@example.com",
      "password": "<skin account password>",
      "player": "Steve"
    }
  }
}
```

- `api`：Yggdrasil API root（例如 Blessing Skin 的 `/api/yggdrasil`）；
- `username` / `password`：客户端登录凭据（邮箱或角色名，取决于 API 实现）；
- `player`：可选；账号有多个角色时必须指定；
- 服务端只需要 `api`，不需要账号密码。

Yggdrasil 模式下顶层 `password` 不再参与握手和密钥派生；旧配置（无 `yggdrasil` 段）行为完全不变。

#### 2. 客户端（client.go / yggdrasil.go）

- 通过 `authserver/authenticate` 登录，多角色时用 `authserver/refresh` 携带 `selectedProfile` 绑定 token；token/clientToken 进程内缓存，`/join` 遇到 403 自动重新登录重试一次。
- Login Start 使用皮肤站返回的真实角色名和 UUID。
- 加密协商完成后按原版算法计算 login hash：

  `sha1(serverId + sharedSecret + serverPublicKey)`，并按 Java `BigInteger#toString(16)` 的二进制补码规则渲染（包含负号和去前导零）。

- **使用 Encryption Request 中实际收到的公钥计算哈希，不再固定配置公钥**；Yggdrasil 模式客户端不需要也不应该去“确认公钥”。
- 用 `accessToken` 真实调用 `sessionserver/session/minecraft/join`。
- 解析 Login Success 的多个 properties，并用 API root 中的 `signaturePublickey` 校验 `textures` 属性签名：
  - SHA1withRSA（与 Blessing Skin 的 `openssl_sign` 默认算法、Minecraft 客户端的签名校验一致）；
  - 支持 PEM / 裸 base64 公钥；
  - 公钥按账号缓存，验签失败时自动重新拉取一次（覆盖皮肤站轮换密钥）；
  - `textures` 缺失、无签名、签名不匹配都会拒绝登录；
  - 校验发生在发送 Login Acknowledged 之前，失败不会进入 play 阶段。
- Yggdrasil 模式不再往 Verify Token 尾部追加预共享密码，保持和原版客户端一致的报文形状。

#### 3. 服务端（server.go）

- Yggdrasil 模式下每个进程随机生成 1024-bit RSA 密钥对（与原版服务端行为一致），**不再从 password 派生**；
- 解密共享密钥后，用自己实际持有的公钥计算同一个 login hash，真实调用 `sessionserver/session/minecraft/hasJoined`；
- 因为客户端 `/join` 与服务端 `/hasJoined` 存在天然竞态，服务端以 200ms 间隔轮询，最长 10s；
- 校验返回的角色 UUID / 名称必须与 Login Start 一致；
- Login Success 直接使用 `hasJoined` 返回的已签名 properties（含 `textures`、`uploadableTextures`）；
- 失败时按原版语义断连：未加入 → `multiplayer.disconnect.unverified_username`，API 异常 → `multiplayer.disconnect.authservers_down`；
- 未配置 `yggdrasil` 时保留原预共享密码 + `profiles` 白名单逻辑。

#### 4. 安全模型与警告

Yggdrasil 模式的安全绑定发生在 Yggdrasil 查询里：中间人两侧分别握手时，客户端提交的 hash 和服务端查询的 hash 必然不同，`hasJoined` 返回空，连接失败；即使不固定服务端公钥也无法完成中间人。

由于这时不再使用预共享密码、也不做密码派生，控制台会在 config 加载时输出一次警告（`errors.LogWarning`）：

```text
XMC: Yggdrasil mode is enabled. The RSA key pair is generated randomly and "password"
is no longer used to derive it or to authenticate the transport; players are verified
through https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil (client /join, server /hasJoined).
Both ends must be able to reach the Yggdrasil API. The configured "password" is ignored.
```

### 兼容性

- 不配置 `yggdrasil`：完全保持旧行为（密码派生密钥 + verify to

issues.title: Fix: resolve bugs, data races and leaks found by a codebase audit
issues.body:
## Summary

A systematic audit of `proxy/`, `app/`, `transport/` and `common/` (connection lifecycles, UDP relays, protocol frame parsing, hot paths) uncovered ~40 verifiable issues. This PR fixes them in small, contained patches.

## Security

- **shadowsocks_2022 UDP (OOM DoS)**: NAT sessions were created *before* authentication and without any cap (`GetOrCreate` on the raw AES-ECB header). ~10k random pkt/s \u2192 ~5M live sessions in the 500s window \u2192 multi-GB heap. Sessions are now created only after the AEAD/EIH check succeeds (`packet.go`, `inbound_multi.go`; `RelayInbound` already validated EIH first and is unchanged).
- **UDP truncation**: `shadowsocks.EncodeUDPPacket` silently truncated datagrams whose header+payload exceeded 8 KB (unchecked `ErrBufferFull`), and hysteria's UDP writer silently dropped messages that did not fit. Both now return an explicit error; trojan's `writePacket` pre-checks the size with a clear error.
- **XtlsFilterTls**: the attacker-controlled session-id length could make the cipher-suite read go past the buffer end (stale pool bytes), flipping `EnableXtls` detection. Bounds-checked now.
- **protocol/address.go**: a zero-length domain (attacker-controlled byte) made `BytesFrom(-0)` return the whole scratch buffer and panic on `domain[0]` \u2014 and the inbound path has no `recover()`. Now rejected with an error.
- **observatory**: `GetObservation` handed the shared, concurrently mutated `[]*OutboundStatus` to all balancers; it now returns a snapshot under `statusLock`.
- **grpc dial**: a failed `grpc.NewClient` stored a nil conn in `globalDialerMap`; the next lookup would panic. Error is now returned before caching.

## Data races (verified with `go test -race`)

- `session.CanSpliceCopy`: written by the downlink task and read by the uplink task (and vice versa); now accessed via `atomic.StoreInt32/LoadInt32` everywhere (47 sites, field documented as atomic-only).
- `tls.Config`: OCSP/hot-reload tickers replaced certificates in the slice while concurrent handshakes read them, and `isCertificateExpired` mutated the shared `Leaf`. Certificates now live in a small `certificateBundle` guarded by an RWMutex; the OCSP callback swaps in a *copy* of the certificate instead of mutating it; `isCertificateExpired` no longer writes.
- `common/cache/lru`: `PeekKeyFromValue` read list elements without the lock (race-detector-confirmed, fakedns hot path); `Put` also left a stale `valueToElement` entry when updating an existing key.
- mux: `x.Status = Active` written without `XUDPManager` lock; hard type assertions in `Session.Close` replaced with a checked one.
- reverse bridge/portal: worker state fields accessed from monitor/heartbeat/picker goroutines; now atomic.
- kcp: `rd`/`wd` deadlines written by `SetDeadline` and read by wait loops; now `atomic.Int64` nanoseconds.
- websocket: `delayDialConn.closed` is atomic now.
- dns outbound: `c.conn` read outside the lock; captured under the lock.
- router webhook: `wg.Add(1)` could race with `Close`\u2019s `wg.Wait()`; Add and the closed check are serialized by a mutex.
- tests (splithttp, blackhole): unsynchronized test state flagged by `-race` fixed.

## Leaks

- splithttp: quic.Transport + UDP socket leaked on every failed H3 dial (fix mirrors masque/xdrive); pooled HTTP/1.1 upload conns were never closed (tracked and closed on `Close()` and on write/read failure).
- mux: the picker's periodic cleanup returned an error when idle, which permanently killed the 30s cleanup task.
- proxyman inbound: `udpWorker.Close()` never closed active UDP sessions (goroutine + pipe per session leaked on every Instance restart).
- dns: with `serveStale` and no `serveExpiredTTL` the cache cleanup never ran \u2014 unbounded growth; cleanup now always runs and evicts entries stale for more than 24h.
- wireguard: device leaked if `IpcSet`/`Up` failed in `Start()`.
- vless: `GetReverse` waited forever for outbound handlers (now bounded, 10s); `testpre` goroutines hot-looped

issues.title: Outbounds: Avoid circular dependencies with the built-in DNS
issues.body:
重写 Lua 文档的时候被迫写了下面加粗的这段，觉得十分不科学，应该把它做成和 targetStrategy 一样防环，没有大的副作用。各出站的行为也比较统一。

> ::: warning 循环依赖
任意查询交给内置 DNS 模块处理时，若选中 DNS 服务器的 `address` 不含 `+local`，则到该服务器的连接会交给路由。若 `address` 是域名，路由脚本可能再次调用内置 DNS 解析它。新的查询可能按 DNS 和路由规则顺利完成，也可能经过多个 DNS 服务器和出站，重新依赖尚未完成的解析，形成死循环。

> 为避免这种潜在的循环依赖，DNS 模块会将自身发起的所有连接标记为 `skipDNSResolve = true`。核心原生的路由模块不检查是否真的成环，而是据此标记简单粗暴地跳过 DNS 解析，直接杜绝成环可能；请求随后继续匹配其余规则并交给出站。Lua 脚本需要自行处理该标记，建议同样跳过解析，也可以按需扩展处理方式。

> **Freedom 出站不会检查 `skipDNSResolve`。若脚本将这类连接交给它，且其 `sockopt.domainStrategy` 非 `AsIs`，就会再次调用内置 DNS 解析该域名。路由脚本无法干预出站的解析，需另行规避，不再赘述；其他出站的 `targetStrategy` 会像路由一样检查该标记跳过解析以避免成环。**

> 其他出站也有另一种成环路径。若代理出站的服务器地址为域名，且 `sockopt.domainStrategy` 非 `AsIs`，出站就会调用内置 DNS 解析该地址。例如，出站 A 依赖 DNS A 的解析结果，而 DNS A 的查询又被送回出站 A，就会形成死循环；也可能先送到出站 B，再因解析 B 的服务器地址而回到 DNS A，形成更长的依赖链。这些出站与 DNS 之间的循环与路由脚本无关，需另行规避，此处不再赘述。

issues.title: gRPC transport: Do not read hunks larger than buf.Size into one buffer
issues.body:
Fixes https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/7369

`HunkReaderWriter.ReadMultiBuffer` (and the multiMode reader) wraps a received hunk in one `Buffer` whenever `cap >= buf.Size`, so a hunk larger than 8192 bytes becomes one oversized buffer. Xray clients never send such hunks, but sing-box writes up to 32 KiB per hunk (its `buf.BufferSize`), and #7369 mentions sing-box clients.

When that buffer reaches a VLESS outbound with `xtls-rprx-vision`, `ReshapeMultiBuffer` copies the tail into a new 8 KiB buffer (`Write` silently drops the rest) and `XtlsPadding` gets `contentLen == 8192`, which gives `paddingLen == -21` and the panic in the issue:

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171]
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.(*Buffer).Extend(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.XtlsPadding(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.(*VisionWriter).WriteMultiBuffer(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.copyInternal(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.Copy(...)
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound.(*Handler).Process.func4()
```

This PR keeps the zero-copy path only for hunks of at most `buf.Size` bytes; larger ones are read into standard buffers.

Reproduced on loopback with a relay like the one in #7369: VLESS gRPC inbound -> VLESS + TLS + Vision outbound -> VLESS Vision server -> echo server. The client writes hunks the way sing-box does and uploads 256 KiB:

| hunk size | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 4096, 8192 | ok | ok |
| 16384, 32768 | relay panics as above | ok, all bytes echoed |
| 32768, multiMode | relay panics as above | ok, all bytes echoed |

The new tests in `transport/internet/grpc/encoding` fail on main with `got a buffer of 8193 bytes, larger than buf.Size`.

issues.title: Feature Request: Add udp+local:// DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)
issues.body:
# Feature Request: Add `udp+local://` DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)

## Summary

Xray's DNS configuration supports `+local` variants for HTTPS, h2c, QUIC and TCP, but there is **no `udp+local` scheme** for plain UDP DNS in local mode. This means there is currently **no way to send plain UDP DNS queries to a local resolver while bypassing the routing/dispatcher stack**.

## Current state

`app/dns/nameserver.go`, `NewServer()` switch (main branch):

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https"):      // DoH remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c"):        // DoH h2c remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https+local"): // DoH local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c+local"):   // DoH h2c local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "quic+local"):  // DoQ local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp"):         // TCP remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp+local"):   // TCP local
case strings.EqualFold(u.String(), "fakedns"):
```

Every protocol except plain UDP has a `+local` form. Plain UDP falls through to the default branch:

```go
if dest.Network == net.Network_UDP {
    return NewClassicNameServer(dest, dispatcher, ...)
}
```

Note that `NewClassicNameServer` receives the `dispatcher`, so plain UDP **always goes through the routing stack** — there is no way to bypass it.

## Why this matters (measured data)

For a local resolver (e.g. smartdns on `127.0.0.1`), bypassing the dispatcher matters. Measured on a local resolver over loopback, one A + one AAAA query for the same domain:

| Path | p50 | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `tcp+local://` (current workaround) | ~810µs | 2 TCP handshakes + 2 closes |
| `tcp+local://` pipelined on 1 conn | ~680µs | would need connection pooling, not implemented |
| **plain UDP, 2 packets sent in parallel** | **~376µs** | no handshake, no teardown |

The UDP path is ~2x faster than the current `tcp+local` workaround because it avoids TCP handshake/teardown entirely. Pairing responses by DNS ID worked in 200/200 trials with zero mismatch.

For users running a local caching resolver, this overhead is paid on every cache-miss lookup.

## Secondary issue: port parsing for bare `udp://` schemes

Related bug found while investigating. With:

```json
"dns": { "servers": ["udp://127.0.0.1:5353"] }
```

xray logs:

```
DNS: created UDP client initialized for udp://127.0.0.1:5353:53
```

The port becomes `5353:53` — the `:5353` is swallowed into the address (as a domain string) and then a default `:53` is appended by:

```go
// app/dns/nameserver_udp.go:41
if address.Port == 0 {
    address.Port = net.Port(53)
}
```

This is because `infra/conf/dns.go` builds the endpoint with `Address` and `Port` as separate fields, and `Address.Build()` calls `net.ParseAddress()` on the whole string including `:5353`, while `Port` stays 0.

Attempting `udp://127.0.0.1` (no port) resolves to `udp://127.0.0.1:53`, which happens to work, but the scheme is still parsed as a domain so the connection fails with:

```
failed to open connection to udp:udp://127.0.0.1:53
> too many colons in address
```

Contrast with `tcp+local`, which parses correctly because it uses `url.Hostname()` and `url.Port()` separately (`app/dns/nameserver_tcp.go:75-81`).

## Proposed change

Add a `udp+local` case that mirrors `tcp+local` — parse host/port via `url.Hostname()` / `url.Port()` and pass `nil` as the dispatcher:

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "udp+local"): // DNS-over-UDP Local mode
    return NewUDPNameServer(u, nil, disableCache, serveStale, serveExpiredTTL, clientIP), nil
```

Where the new constructor resolves the destination the same way `baseTCPNameServer` does:

```go
port := net.Port(53)
if url.Port() != "" {
    if port, err = net.PortFromString(url.Port()); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
}
dest := net.UDPDestination(net.ParseAddress(url.Hostname()), port)
```

This would also give users a documented way to hit a local resolver on a non-53 port without the address-swallowing bug.

## Environment

issues.title: XDRIVE: when the client disappears mid-download, the server uploads the rest of the response and keeps the session for minutes
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [X] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [X] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [X] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

**Cause**

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. XDRIVE has no peer liveness signal: no heartbeat, no idle timeout. `Conn.receive` blocks on the reader channel (`conn.go:53-61`), `walReader.poll` returns quietly on an empty listing (`wal.go:295-297`), `holeTimeout` fires only when later segments exist (`wal.go:312-321`), EOF comes only from a `.end` object (`wal.go:365`).
- No backpressure: `walWriter.Write` appends to the buffer and `flushLocked` starts `go w.upload` (`wal.go:73-91`, `wal.go:127-156`); the semaphore in `upload` limits concurrent `Put`s, not unconsumed data (`wal.go:161-166`). Segments are deleted only by the peer's reader, so nothing limits what

issues.title: XMC: native frame padding and delay range
issues.body:
Follow-up to #6769 (merged in `5d17b872`): completes the remaining `delay` requirement and, per [this reply](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7402#issuecomment-6890345279), switches padding to the more realistic wire format even though that is a breaking change.

## Delay

- `delay` is now a **string**: `"100"` or `"50-150"` (milliseconds). A number written against #6769 no longer parses, so this is a configuration-level breaking change as well.
- The sender waits a uniformly sampled value in `[min, max]` after its turn.
- The receiver waits at least `min` after each turn, including the last one, before the proxy stream starts.
- `config.proto`: `delay` becomes `delay_min` / `delay_max`; negative, reversed and duration-overflowing ranges are rejected at config load.
- `infra/conf`: parses the string delay; tests cover fixed values, ranges and invalid forms.

## Native frame padding (`ea2c7edc`, breaking)

The opaque format wrote a length field that includes its own varint. A vanilla server therefore split the stream one header short and had to take the protocol pipeline over — something a Fabric server mod cannot do without affecting ordinary players.

- One padding chunk becomes one or more configuration-state custom payload frames on `xmc:pad`; the length field now has the vanilla meaning (bytes after the field).
- Chunks above the 32767-byte serverbound payload limit are split; captured 2-byte turns send the smallest possible frame.
- Nothing reads padding any more: it is ordinary traffic that the next reader drops as an unknown packet. Both ends only send and apply the configured pauses.
- The first turn still counts the two Login Acknowledged bytes as its prefix; they are not repeated.
- `maxPacketDataLength` is raised from 32 KiB to 1 MiB (vanilla's clientbound custom payload limit), which a real configuration state can reach with registry data.

**Breaking:** both ends must run this version. No proto field was added for padding; the `paddings` length/direction semantics are unchanged, and `delay` moved from a number to a millisecond string.

Example:

```json
"paddings": [
  {"length": "44", "direction": "c2s", "delay": "0"},
  {"length": "64-128", "direction": "s2c", "delay": "100"},
  {"length": "25", "direction": "c2s", "delay": "50-150"},
  {"length": "32768-49152", "direction": "s2c"}
]
```

Both endpoints should still use the same array and the same `delay` ranges, because that is what reproduces the captured shape. Nothing is compared against the peer's schedule any more, though: the receiver does not consume padding, so a length, direction or turn-count difference can no longer fail or stall the handshake, it only changes what each side sends.

## Scope

Per the cleanup in #6769, this PR does **not** restore the XMC `README.md` / `*_test.go` files deleted in that squash commit. The only new test file is `padding_frames_test.go`, which covers the frame plan/reachability and the source of the padding stream, because the wire format changed here.

## Tests

```text
go test -count=1 ./infra/conf
go test -count=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc
go build -o /tmp/xray-core-build ./main
go run ./infra/vformat -pwd . -mode check
go run ./infra/vprotogen -pwd . -mode check
```

## Validation fix

A legacy password longer than 113 bytes is now rejected when the configuration is built (`035c45de`), instead of being accepted and then failing every handshake: the verify token plus the password must fit one RSA-1024 PKCS#1 v1.5 block (128-11 bytes), so `rsa.EncryptPKCS1v15` was failing on the client and the server could not decrypt it either.

```text
go test -count=1 ./infra/conf ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc
```

issues.title: XMC finalmask: Yggdrasil third-party login and texture verification
issues.body:
Refs #7394 (proposal). **Draft for review, not ready to merge.**

## What this adds

- **Yggdrasil third-party login.** The XMC client can authenticate against a third-party Yggdrasil API (Blessing Skin / authlib-injector compatible), join the Minecraft session with the standard vanilla login hash and reuse the API's signed textures. The XMC server verifies players through `sessionserver/session/minecraft/hasJoined` instead of a hand-copied profile list.
- **Texture verification and key handling.** In Yggdrasil mode the RSA key pair is no longer derived from the password: each side generates its own key pair, the client accepts the key sent in Encryption Request and binds it through the session hash, and the server verifies with its own actual public key through `/hasJoined`. The client verifies the signed `textures` property with the API's `signaturePublickey` (SHA1withRSA), refreshing the key once if a rotation is detected.
- **Chore:** `config.pb.go` regenerated with `infra/vprotogen`, because the checked-in file carried `protoc v7.36.1` while the tool records `(unknown)`, which made `-mode check` fail.

Files: `yggdrasil.go` (new), `client.go`, `server.go`, `profile.go`, `config.go`, `config.proto` (`Config.yggdrasil = 13`), `infra/conf/transport_finalmask.go`, plus tests.

## Compatibility

- No `yggdrasil` section: the legacy pre-shared password + `profiles` path is unchanged.
- With `yggdrasil`: `password` is ignored (a console warning is printed) and `profiles` is not required.

issues.title: XMC: bound padding schedules and allow disabling padding
issues.body:
Draft: stacked on #7402, whose padding-frame and compression commits are included in this branch. After #7402 merges I will rebase onto `main` and the diff here reduces to one commit (`0ec2360c`).

Follow-up to #7402 and to [the remaining items in this comment](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7402#issuecomment-6886742322).

## Padding pauses are cancellable and bounded

A padding turn can configure a pause, and the schedule used to `time.Sleep` through it:
a connection closed during a pause kept its handshake goroutine asleep, and a schedule whose pauses add up to more than the two-minute handshake deadline could never complete. A configuration could also declare any number of turns.

- Padding pauses are now timers that also watch a per-connection `done` channel, which `Close` closes. Closing a connection stops the schedule immediately.
- A configured schedule is rejected at build time when it has more than 256 turns, more than 64 MiB of turns in total, or more than the handshake timeout minus ten seconds of pauses in total. These bounds are far above the captured preset (39 turns, about 1.1 MiB of server-to-client turns, about 200 ms of pauses).
- `delay` range semantics, which the comment asked to confirm: the side that sends a turn samples `[delay_min, delay_max]` and pauses that long after its own turn, so the jitter is on the sender's side; the peer only knows `delay_min` and pauses that long before its next own turn. The proto comment now says this explicitly.

## Padding can be disabled explicitly

`paddings: []` still meant "use the preset", with no way to turn padding off. Now:

- an absent `paddings` keeps the built-in preset;
- an explicit empty `paddings` array disables padding (the new `no_padding` proto field carries that across the wire, because an unset repeated field cannot express it);
- `"noPadding": true` does the same in JSON, and combining it with a non-empty `paddings` is a configuration error.

## Not changed here

- **Custom `paddings` replace the whole preset, including the Play-state tail.** This is a policy decision: either the array is the complete schedule (today), or the tail stays and the array only replaces the startup turns. I would keep today's behavior, because a user who captured their own login is the one who should decide the tail.
- **Early-arrival detection.** This became impossible to observe here: since #7402 the receiver does not read padding, so it has nothing to compare against the expected turn. The equivalent safeguard is the pause bound above, which keeps a stalled peer inside the handshake deadline.

## Tests

```text
go test -count=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc ./infra/conf
go test -count=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/...
go build -o /tmp/xray ./main
go run ./infra/vformat -pwd . -mode check
go run ./infra/vprotogen -pwd . -mode check
```

New coverage: pauses return on `Close` (both the runner and a real `clientConn`), the three schedule limits, disabled padding (absent vs empty array vs `noPadding`, plus the conflict), and an end-to-end run with `paddings: []` on both ends.

This PR was produced with AI assistance (DeepSeek Harness).

issues.title: XHTTP: Synchronize QUIC test shutdown
issues.body:
## Why

`Test_ListenXHAndDial_QUIC` writes `serverClosed` from its server goroutine and reads it from the test goroutine. Sleeping for 100 ms after closing the client leaves those accesses unsynchronized. The Go race detector reports the read and write on clean `main` (`c4561418`).

## Change

Signal completion through a channel after the server handler closes its connection. Wait for the signal within the existing five-second test deadline. The patch changes only the test.

## Verification

- The standalone QUIC test passed 10 consecutive runs on Windows amd64 with Go 1.27.0.
- With #7348 applied locally to address the independent TLS certificate race, `go test -race -timeout=90s -count=5 ./transport/internet/splithttp ./transport/internet/httpupgrade` passed. The draft targets `main` directly.

issues.title: XDRIVE: Prevent ring-slot reuse before the previous upload completes
issues.body:
## Problem

The peer can acknowledge segment 0 from the inline session announcement while its upload to the ring is still in flight. With a ring of depth 2, that acknowledgement can admit the upload for segment 2 to the same slot. If the original upload finishes last, it overwrites segment 2 and leaves a gap in the stream.

This ordering reproduces the intermittent `TestSlotFirstAnnouncement` failure seen in two Ubuntu jobs. [November 13 job](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/actions/runs/43400976127/job/131803491599) and [November 14 job](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/actions/runs/43647865009/job/132609573715).

## Fix

- Require a successful previous write to the same slot and an acknowledgement from the existing cumulative watermark before reusing it.
- Keep checking the watermark while the local upload is pending. The reader-stall timeout applies while the acknowledgement is missing, so an acknowledged upload can finish retrying during `Close`.
- Propagate a terminal write error to queued reuse of the slot and retain the best-effort error frame for peers still waiting for that sequence.

The change uses the existing announcement, frame format, and acknowledgement protocol.

## Validation

- Extended `TestSlotFirstAnnouncement` to hold the first upload after the inline acknowledgement. The slow-write case verifies the complete byte stream through EOF. The failure case verifies that `Close` promptly returns the original write error and that the slot contains the error frame.
- Verified that the regression test detects premature reuse on upstream `main`. Both cases passed 100 times with the race detector on this branch.
- Passed the full `transport/internet/xdrive` suite on Windows with and without `-race`. Live cloud tests were skipped.

issues.title: UDP: avoid info-level read failure after local session termination
issues.body:
When the UDP idle timer or owner closes a session while `handleInput` is reading, termination cancels the context and interrupts the pipe. The read can return `io.ErrClosedPipe` after the loop's context check, producing an info-level `failed to handle UDP input` message for a local close.

Downgrade that error to debug only when this connection's local termination flag is set. Make the existing flag atomic because termination, input handling, and dispatcher reuse inspect it across goroutines. Unrelated read errors, closed-pipe errors without local termination, and parent cancellation alone retain the existing logging behavior. EOF handling and cleanup order are unchanged.

Tests exercise the real pipe interruption path, idle timeout, concurrent/repeated close, wrapped errors, unrelated errors during shutdown, parent cancellation, EOF, and the close callback count. The regression test fails on unmodified main with the original info-level message.

Validation on Windows/amd64:
- `go test ./transport/internet/udp -count=1` passed.
- `go test ./transport/internet/udp -run TestHandleInputTermination -count=100` passed.
- `go vet ./transport/internet/udp` and `git diff --check` passed.

Refs #4621. This addresses local UDP termination only; it does not suppress remote resets or change general connection-error handling.

issues.title: XDRIVE: Cancel pending storage operations on interrupt
issues.body:
## Problem

`common.Interrupt` falls back to `Close()` for an XDRIVE connection. `Close()` drains the writer before canceling the connection context. If storage is holding an upload, interruption waits for the very operation it needs to cancel. The asynchronous slot announcement also uses a background context, so it can remain pending after connection shutdown.

svlavr reported both behaviors while testing direct VLESS multiplexing. A mock backend reproduced them with a held upload and a held announcement. [Original report in #7415](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7415#issuecomment-6886431076)

## Design

`Interrupt()` cancels the session before entering the existing `Close()` path. Cancellation runs before the `sync.Once` guard, so it can wake a graceful close that is already waiting. Both slot and WAL writers stop admitting work after cancellation and wait for in-flight writes to finish unwinding before storage is released. A canceled drain skips the EOF marker.

The slot announcement now uses the session context and is part of the writer’s existing wait group. The context makes an interrupted publication cancelable. Joining it also lets a short graceful transfer finish publishing its session before `Close()` sends EOF and releases storage. This keeps the inline first-segment optimization and the existing wire format.

`Close()` still means graceful drain. Transport owners use `common.Interrupt` on the underlying connection when they need to abort. The direct Mux proposal already unwraps stats connections on its explicit interrupt path. [#7364](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7364)

## Validation

- Added regressions for interrupting an already-running `Close()` with a blocked slot or WAL upload, canceling a pending announcement, and allowing the announcement to finish during graceful close. All four cases detect the original behavior on upstream `main`.
- Passed the full XDRIVE suite on Windows with and without `-race`, plus 50 race-enabled repetitions of the shutdown regressions.
- Trial-merged this branch with #7415 and ran both sets of regressions together 10 times under `-race`. Live cloud tests were skipped.

issues.title: Routing: add server-only VMess UUID routes and online user cache
issues.body:
Allow ordinary VMess clients to select declared server-side routes by changing UUID bytes 7 and 8, with only the server upgraded and no account flag required. `userRoute` is the shared routing matcher; `vlessRoute` keeps its existing behavior.

README.md is unchanged in the PR diff.

## Behavior and compatibility

- Generate aliases only for explicit `routing.rules[].userRoute` values applicable to the inbound and user, including existing exact/regexp user matching. Destination-dependent conditions remain routing conditions; Lua-only routing declares no aliases.
- Preserve exact configured UUIDs and the original account's email, policy, statistics and API identity. The experimental account flag and wire extension have been removed completely. Account JSON/protobuf definitions and client encoding match the pre-feature source; no account option or wire field is added.
- Admit connections after normal authenticated header checks. Registration IDs, route generations and pending-change checks reject stale candidates across account/rule changes, including removal and re-addition of the same account object. Closed validators cannot rebuild catalogs.
- Retain identity history during an inbound's lifetime so a removed exact credential cannot become another user's generated alias. Different original route bytes mark the 14-byte identity ambiguous and disable its aliases. Exact credentials remain usable. History is not persisted: independently revocable users and credential rotations must use distinct non-route UUID bytes.
- Align Unicode email removal with the inbound's lowercase index. Retain AuthID replay entries for the full inclusive timestamp-validity interval using 241-second buckets; accepted clock skew and wire encoding remain unchanged. This retains more replay records under sustained traffic.

## Cache and resource bounds

Only authenticated online/recent accounts populate the prepared cache; there are no IP/source-address hints. Idempotent connection leases expire two minutes after the final close. Route changes preserve live leases and idle deadlines without refreshing recency. Search and eviction share one recency list, immutable provider declarations are copied before filtering, and rejected cache growth does not evict unrelated entries.

Per inbound: 64 MiB prepared-key payload, a 128 MiB raw-alias-key limit, and two concurrent alias scans. Oversized live catalogs preserve exact credentials while rejecting aliases. Metadata, replay records and temporary old/new catalog overlap are additional memory. Occupied scan slots can reject further alias handshakes, including hot-cache users; exact credentials bypass those slots.

The amd64 AES-NI/SSE4.1 search accelerator retains all ten AES rounds in a 68-byte schedule and rechecks candidates with the standard-library decoder. Unsupported CPUs, `purego`, and Go FIPS mode select the standard-library fallback. This is not a cryptographic certification or a claim of VLESS-equivalent lookup cost.

## Validation

- VMess, router/command, routing features and configuration tests passed, along with the complete VMess `purego` tests and repository formatting.
- After removing the experimental account flag, all 160 published-binary compatibility cases passed again using clients 1.8.24, 25.12.8 and 26.11.9: 120 ordinary VMess/VLESS cases in both directions, 33 UUID-only/negative/legacy-route cases, and seven byte-identical old-config compilation cases. Coverage includes TCP/UDP, AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305, Mux, and route values 0/300/65535.
- Known-answer AES plus 4,096 differential decryptions; malformed headers and replay; identity collisions/revocation; concurrent account/rule changes; and 4,000-operation cache lifecycle checks passed. Selected regressions also passed 30 repetitions at each of 1/2/4 CPUs with shuffled order, Go pointer checking, and runtime CPU-feature fallback.
- Windows executable and Linux amd64/arm64 VMess cross-builds passed. The full network scenario package passed

issues.title: Routing: Add `RegisterProcessFinder` for `process` on all platforms
issues.body:
The routing rule `process` calls `net.FindProcess` for each new connection. The lookup keeps no cache:

- On Windows, each call gets the full TCP or UDP table from the system.
- On Linux, each call reads the socket tables in `/proc/net`. Then it reads the links in `/proc/<pid>/fd` of each process.

With many sockets, each call is slow. A benchmark opened 100 or 1000 TCP connections on 127.0.0.1. Each connection has two sockets. Then the benchmark measured `net.FindProcess` for the client socket of the last connection. It ran with Xray-core v26.10.31 in two VMs with 2 virtual CPUs: Windows 10 22H2 and Ubuntu 26.04. On Linux, it ran as root.

| System | Sockets | Median | 99th percentile |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows | 200 | 186 µs | 285 µs |
| Windows | 2000 | 2.06 ms | 3.57 ms |
| Linux | 200 | 3.09 ms | 3.53 ms |
| Linux | 2000 | 8.87 ms | 9.61 ms |

An application that embeds Xray-core can use a faster method of its platform, for example netlink `sock_diag` on Linux. It can also keep a cache of the socket tables between connections. A hook gives the application this choice. The lookup of each platform stays as it is. On Android, an application can already register its own finder with `RegisterAndroidProcessFinder`.

This pull request adds such a hook for all platforms:

- `net.RegisterProcessFinder(f)` replaces the lookup of the platform with `f`. A nil finder restores the lookup of the platform.
- `net.FindProcess` calls the registered finder. Without a registered finder, it calls the lookup of the platform, as before.
- Xray-core can call the finder from many goroutines at the same time. Thus the finder must be safe for concurrent use.
- If an application registers both finders on Android, `net.FindProcess` calls only the finder of `RegisterProcessFinder`. `RegisterAndroidProcessFinder` stays as it is.
- The lookup of each platform has the new name `findProcess`. Its code has no other change.

Without a registered finder, the behavior does not change. With the hook, each call loads one atomic pointer. `TestRegisterProcessFinder` tests the hook.

issues.title: Feature request: configurable TLS fingerprint selection with weights and an explicit allowlist
issues.body:
As one of many VPN services using Xray, we’d find it useful to configure multiple TLS fingerprints, assign each a percentage (chance of choosing specific fingerprint on connection, analogous to `random`), and explicitly exclude fingerprints that do not work in our target networks. The core would select a fingerprint once per new connection according to those weights.

For example: **Firefox 9%, Chrome 70%, Edge 12%, Safari 9%**, with `ios`, `android`, and `chrome-133` excluded.

In our experience, Russian DPI blocks connections using those three fingerprints in some cases. Unrestricted random selection is therefore risky: individual connections may fail simply because an incompatible fingerprint was selected.

We previously used Firefox because it worked well in our environment. However, what works today may change, and having 100% of connections share the same normalized TLS fingerprint could itself help TSPU identify VPN traffic.

Weighted selection would reduce this uniformity, while explicit control over the allowed fingerprints would help preserve reliability. This would not make VPN traffic indistinguishable from browsers, but it would give operators a practical way to manage that tradeoff.

issues.title: Routing: Fix Linux `process` for IPv4-mapped sockets
issues.body:
On Linux, a `process` rule misses IPv4 connections made from IPv6 (dual-stack) sockets, which Java and .NET open by default. Such a socket is listed in `/proc/net/tcp6` or `udp6` with an IPv4-mapped address, but for an IPv4 source the lookup reads only `/proc/net/tcp` and compares the IPv4 form. It is #6533 on Linux.

Fix: for an IPv4 source, also look for its IPv4-mapped address in the IPv6 file.

Test: `TestFindProcessIPv4Mapped` fails on main for TCP and UDP. With a real Java program through a SOCKS inbound, `"process": ["java"]` is skipped on main and matches with the fix.

issues.title: XHTTP/3 client: Close the UDP socket when the QUIC dial fails
issues.body:
When an XHTTP/3 dial fails, e.g. where QUIC is blocked, the `quic.Transport` made for it and its UDP socket are never closed. Each failed dial leaves one socket and two goroutines, so a client that keeps retrying runs out of file descriptors.

Fix: close both when `DialEarly` fails, as the MASQUE and XDRIVE dialers do. The socket goes first: `tr.Close()` waits for its read to return, which over `dialerProxy` would block the dial.

Test: `Test_DialQUICFailureClosesSocket` fails on main. 100 dials to a peer that never answers leave 100 sockets and 200 goroutines on main, none with the fix.

issues.title: Observatory: return independent snapshots under the status lock
issues.body:
`Observer.GetObservation` returns the internal status slice and its protobuf objects while background probes update and prune them. Callers can therefore observe changes after the method returns, race with updates during serialization, or accidentally mutate observer state.

Clone the observation under the existing status mutex. The returned message owns its slice, status objects, and nested messages; serialization happens after the lock is released. Probe scheduling, balancing behavior, and the protobuf API are unchanged.

Tests cover preservation of fields, snapshot stability after updates/additions/pruning, caller mutation of the slice and nested HealthPing message, empty results, and concurrent updates/pruning/readers/serialization. The isolation regression fails on unmodified main.

- Windows: Observatory package tests, 100 repetitions of the new snapshot tests, balancer regression tests, and `go vet ./app/observatory/...` passed.

Validation run: https://github.com/wywywywycloud/Xray-core/actions/runs/43646303751

Refs #5117. This fixes snapshot safety in the existing Observatory API; it does not implement the remaining outbound-management features.

issues.title: conf: support process-scoped fingerprint weights in TLS
issues.body:
Adds `tlsSettings.fingerprintWeights`, resolving an explicit weighted browser policy once per process into the existing protobuf `Fingerprint` field. New TCP connections, HTTP clients, and reconnects reuse the selected profile. Equivalent policies share the process-wide result from the common resolver.

**Depends on #7406; merge #7406 first.** This branch is based directly on the resolver branch and does **not** depend on REALITY PR #7407. Until #7406 is merged, GitHub's main-branch diff also includes that dependency. Review TLS-only changes in [this comparison](https://github.com/wywywywycloud/Xray-core/compare/codex/weighted-fingerprint-resolver...codex/tls-weighted-fingerprints). Related: #7405 (selection lifetime revised to once per process).

Example fragment inside `tlsSettings`:

```json
"fingerprintWeights": {
  "firefox": 9,
  "chrome": 70,
  "edge": 12,
  "safari": 9
}
```

Weights are relative probabilities per process, not proportions of connections. The field conflicts with a nonempty `fingerprint`; invalid policies fail before selection. Resolution occurs after TLS configuration checks succeed, with debug logging of the selected name. Existing single-fingerprint/default/random behavior and protobuf definitions remain unchanged. TLS transport call sites consume the resolved name through their existing paths; no handshake or ALPN rewriting behavior is changed. XDRIVE's ALPN warning now examines the built TLS configuration, including the selected profile.

Supported paths include RAW, gRPC, WebSocket, HTTPUpgrade, XHTTP/XDRIVE over TCP, MASQUE H2, and FinalMask XDNS HTTPS over TCP. Configuration checks reject paths that cannot apply uTLS profiles: mKCP, Hysteria, XHTTP/XDRIVE H3, MASQUE's QUIC path (including its default), XDNS H3 or non-HTTPS resolvers, and Realm's Go TLS client. The checks match each transport's actual ALPN switch rather than rejecting every list containing h3.

Browser dialer is rejected for weighted WebSocket/XHTTP configurations when configured or active at build time. Embedders can enable it later through Reload; since it then owns the handshake, the browser path emits a once-per-process warning that Xray fingerprint settings do not apply. This warning also covers legacy fingerprint settings; it does not block or reconfigure browser connections. No runtime policy metadata is added to protobuf.

Unlike modern REALITY's additional hybrid-key-share requirement, ordinary TLS supports all four example aliases in the local integration tests, including Edge. This does not guarantee acceptance by any particular remote server or DPI. Aliases retain their existing uTLS-version semantics.

Validation (Go 1.27.4, Windows amd64):

- `go test ./infra/conf -run "TestTLSFingerprintWeights|TestXDriveHTTP1ALPNWarning" -count=1 -timeout 90s`
- `go test ./infra/conf ./transport/internet/tls ./transport/internet/browser_dialer ./transport/internet/websocket ./transport/internet/splithttp ./transport/internet/xdrive ./transport/internet/finalmask/xdns -count=1 -timeout 120s`
- `git diff --check`

New tests cover normalized-policy stability, equivalence to a selected legacy configuration, invalid inputs/conflicts, unchanged legacy modes, no selection on invalid TLS configuration, transport propagation and rejection, browser configuration, nested XDNS, Realm rejection, and XDRIVE warnings with/without ECH. A local certificate-pinned TLS/HTTP integration test verifies each of Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari across two fresh connections. All listed tests passed. The race detector was not run locally (no C compiler installed).

issues.title: conf: support process-scoped fingerprint weights in REALITY
issues.body:
Adds client-side `realitySettings.fingerprintWeights`. Configuration building validates all candidates, resolves the policy once per process using the shared resolver, and stores the selected name in the existing protobuf `Fingerprint` field. Reconnecting does not reselect; RAW, XHTTP and gRPC use their existing REALITY client path.

**Depends on #7406; merge #7406 first.** This branch is stacked on its resolver commit. Until that dependency is merged, the GitHub diff against main also includes PR 1. The REALITY-only changes can be reviewed in [this comparison](https://github.com/wywywywycloud/Xray-core/compare/codex/weighted-fingerprint-resolver...codex/reality-weighted-fingerprints). ```json

```json
  "firefox": 15,
  "chrome": 70,
  "safari": 15
}
```

The new field conflicts with a nonempty `fingerprint` and is rejected in server configurations. Selection happens only after the remaining client configuration checks succeed. Debug logging identifies the selected name. Existing single-fingerprint/default/random behavior, protobuf definitions, and connection code are unchanged.

The current pinned REALITY server additionally requires an X25519MLKEM768 share before standalone X25519; the new weighted mode validates that requirement as well. No network connections are made during validation.

**Compatibility finding:** the currently pinned uTLS `edge` alias is Edge 85 and lacks the required hybrid share. Consequently the earlier illustrative Firefox 9 / Chrome 70 / Edge 12 / Safari 9 policy is rejected, with a candidate-specific error, instead of producing intermittent failures. issues.title: conf: add process-scoped weighted fingerprint resolver
issues.body:
Adds a shared configuration-layer resolver for explicit, weighted browser fingerprint policies. Each normalized policy selects once per process and reuses that result across subsequent resolutions. This is groundwork for TLS and REALITY configuration support; it does not expose a new JSON setting in those configurations yet.

Related to #7405. This implements the revised selection lifetime: **once per process per distinct policy**, rather than once per connection as originally described in the issue.

Equivalent policies share a cached result regardless of key order, name casing, or proportional scaling of weights. Distinct policies select independently. Positive uint64 weights are checked for overflow; unknown names, duplicate normalized names, and special random/randomized/Go TLS/unsafe modes are rejected. Browser aliases and explicit registered browser versions are accepted. Aliases retain their existing uTLS version semantics.

Validation is separate from selection. Selection uses crypto/rand without modulo bias, serializes concurrent initialization, and does not cache entropy failures or fall back to a default profile. The process-lifetime cache intentionally retains each resolved policy until process exit. Existing GetFingerprint and the startup-selected random preset are unchanged.

Future TLS/REALITY integrations can validate their transport-specific constraints, resolve the policy, and write the selected name into the existing protobuf Fingerprint field. Those integrations, transport compatibility checks, user-facing documentation, and protobuf policy support are outside this PR.

Validation (Go 1.27.4, Windows amd64):

issues.title: XDRIVE: retry WAL segments that are visible before upload completes
Tunnel inbound: Close idle fake UDP sockets in TPROXY mode
issues.body:
Fixes #5263 (closed as not planned).

### Problem

With `tproxy` on a Tunnel (dokodemo-door) inbound, replies go through `PacketWriter`. It opens a fake UDP socket bound to each remote address that sends a reply ([dokodemo.go:231-245](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L231-L245)). The sockets are closed only in `Close()` ([:266-273](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L266-L273)), when the UDP session ends ([:189](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L189)).

A cone session ends after its client port has been silent for 2 minutes ([worker.go:397](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go#L397)). Only client packets count as activity ([worker.go:200](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go#L200)). A P2P application sends from one port to many peers and is never silent for 2 minutes. Its session keeps one fake socket for every peer that ever replied.

On a router with transparent proxy (TPROXY → dokodemo-door) xray grew by about 1450 sockets and 7 MB of RSS per hour: 6524 open fds 4.5 hours after a restart that followed an OOM kill. #5263 shows the same growth.

### Reproduction

`05-xray-fakeudp-repro.sh` (below) runs as a normal user in network namespaces: `unshare -Urn sh 05-xray-fakeudp-repro.sh ./xray 10 300`. The client sends from one UDP port to 10 new peers per second. Every 10th datagram goes to a peer first contacted more than 180 s ago. Peers echo from the address they were sent to. Inbound:

```json
{"listen": "0.0.0.0", "port": 1100, "protocol": "tunnel",
 "settings": {"allowedNetwork": "udp", "followRedirect": true},
 "streamSettings": {"sockopt": {"tproxy": "tproxy"}}}
```

```sh
iptables -t mangle -A PREROUTING -i <client-if> -p udp -j TPROXY --on-port 1100 --tproxy-mark 1
ip rule add fwmark 1 lookup 100
ip route add local 0.0.0.0/0 dev lo table 100
```

### Results

`main` at c456141, linux/amd64, 10 new peers/s, open fds of the xray process:

| time, s | main | with this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 60 | 609 | 609 |
| 120 | 1209 | 1209 |
| 180 | 1809 | 1508 |
| 240 | 2349 | 1501 |
| 300 | 2888 | 1495 |

Both builds: 3000/3000 replies, 120/120 replies from old peers, none from a wrong address.

Router, arm64, v26.7.28 with the same change: 6524 fds and growing before; about 880 without a trend 15 hours later, 575 five days later.

### Change

- `PacketWriter` records when each remote last sent a reply.
- `WriteMultiBuffer`, at most every 30 s, closes and forgets the fake sockets of remotes silent for 2 minutes. The next reply from such a remote opens a new socket through the existing path.
- The socket of the original destination (`w.conn`) is never closed early. Datagrams without a `UDP` address are written to it too ([:255](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L255)). Before, one write error on it closed it for the rest of the session.
- On a write error the map entry is deleted instead of set to `nil`.

The sweep runs on the writer goroutine: no new goroutine, no lock. 2 minutes matches the session timeout in `worker.go`. If replies stop completely, the sweep waits for the next write, which is the old behavior.

### Tests

- `TestSweepIdleClosesOnlyIdleFakeSockets` in `proxy/dokodemo/fakeudp_sweep_test.go`.
- `go build ./...`, `go test ./proxy/dokodemo/...` (also `-race`), `go vet ./proxy/dokodemo/`, `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check` pass with go1.27.0.

# Fake UDP socket growth in Tunnel inbound (TPROXY), reproduction.
# Run as a normal user:  unshare -Urn sh 05-xray-fakeudp-repro.sh /path/to/xray [RATE] [SECONDS]

issues.title: Observatory: fix data race in observation results
issues.body:
## Summary

Fix a data race in ordinary Observatory's `GetObservation` by returning an independent snapshot of the observation results.

## Problem

`GetObservation` currently returns a new `ObservationResult` containing references to the observer's internal status slice and messages.

Background probes update these statuses under `statusLock`, while consumers may read or serialize them after `GetObservation` returns.

This can cause concurrent reads and writes in routing strategies, metrics, and gRPC protobuf serialization.

The issue was reproduced on the current upstream `main` with Go's race detector, including a protobuf serialization error:

```text
WARNING: DATA RACE
size mismatch: calculated=22, measured=31
```

## Solution

Deep-clone the observation result while holding the existing `statusLock`:

```go
o.statusLock.Lock()
defer o.statusLock.Unlock()

return proto.Clone(&ObservationResult{Status: o.status}), nil
```

This ensures that callers receive an independent snapshot, including nested protobuf messages and unknown fields.

The existing synchronization mechanism, protobuf API, health checks, and routing behavior remain unchanged.

## Testing

Added two regression tests:

- **Snapshot isolation:** verifies that returned results do not share mutable state with the observer or other snapshots, including nested messages and unknown fields.
- **Concurrent access:** exercises status updates, additions, removals, and concurrent reads with protobuf serialization.

Both tests reproduce the original issue. The snapshot test also fails when using a mutex without deep copying.

Validation completed successfully:

- `go test -race ./app/observatory/...`
- `go test ./app/observatory/... ./app/router/... ./app/metrics/...`
- Xray build
- Formatting and diff checks

## Performance

Deep cloning introduces O(n) copying under the existing mutex. Benchmarks covering 2, 20, and 200 outbound statuses confirm the expected linear cost.

The fix intentionally favors correctness and minimal changes over additional synchronization complexity.
